q: What is the fan-shaped area of land called where a river splits into channels before meeting the sea?
fact: It is named after the Greek letter delta, whose triangle shape matches the mouth of the Nile.

q: What is the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth, at 0 degrees latitude, called?
fact: At the equator, day and night each last about 12 hours all year round.

q: What is land joined to the mainland but almost surrounded by water, like Italy or Florida, called?
fact: The word comes from the Latin 'paene insula', meaning 'almost an island'.

q: What is the cold, treeless plain of the Arctic called, where the ground below the surface stays frozen all year?
fact: The frozen layer underground is called permafrost. In the short summer only the top layer thaws, and the land fills with flowers.

q: Which classical dance form, performed in pointe shoes and tutus, began at the royal courts of Italy and France?
fact: Many of its terms are still French, like plie and pirouette, because King Louis XIV founded the first dance academy in Paris in 1661.

q: What is a long, narrow sea inlet between steep cliffs, carved by a glacier, like those along this country's coast, called?
fact: The longest, Sognefjord, reaches more than 200 km inland and is over 1,300 m deep in places.

q: What is the longest river in this country, famous for the royal chateaux along its valley?
fact: It runs about 1,000 km, and its valley, with castles like Chambord and Amboise, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: Which mountain range stretches across eight countries, including Switzerland, Austria and Italy?
fact: Great rivers including the Rhine, the Rhone and the Po begin in its glaciers and snowfields.

q: Which mountain range curves in a great arc through Slovakia, Ukraine and Romania?
fact: Its forests hold some of Europe's largest populations of brown bears, wolves and lynx.

q: Which saffron-colored rice dish from Valencia is cooked in a wide, shallow pan?
fact: The name comes from the Valencian word for the pan itself. The original version uses rabbit, chicken and beans, not seafood.

q: Which long, thin loaf of bread with a crisp crust is a symbol of France?
fact: In 2022 UNESCO added the craft and culture of making it to its list of intangible heritage.

q: Which white, crumbly cheese, kept in salty brine, is made in Greece mostly from sheep's milk?
fact: Since 2002 only cheese made in Greece in the traditional way may be sold under this name in the European Union.

q: Which Scottish dish of sheep's heart, liver and oats is served on Burns Night?
fact: Burns Night, on January 25, honors the poet Robert Burns, who wrote a whole poem addressed to the dish.

q: Which passionate Andalusian art of song, guitar and dance is famous for stamping feet and hand clapping?
fact: UNESCO added it to its list of intangible heritage in 2010. The hand clapping has its own name: palmas.

q: Which turning ballroom dance in three-four time swept the dance halls of Vienna in the 1800s?
fact: At first many people found it shocking, because partners held each other so closely.

q: Which triangle-shaped, three-stringed instrument is a symbol of Russian folk music?
fact: It comes in several sizes, from the small prima to the huge contrabass, which stands on the floor.

q: Which huge stone amphitheater in Rome, finished in AD 80, could hold about 50,000 spectators?
fact: Its official name was the Flavian Amphitheater. Its nickname may come from a giant statue that stood nearby.

q: Which Moorish palace and fortress, with fountains and carved courtyards, overlooks the city of Granada?
fact: Its name comes from Arabic for 'the red one', after the color of its walls.

q: Which wind instrument, with a bag and droning pipes, is a symbol of Scotland?
fact: The player blows air into the bag and squeezes it with one arm, so the music never stops for a breath.

q: Which royal palace near Paris, home of the famous Hall of Mirrors, did Louis XIV make his seat of power?
fact: Louis XIV turned his father's hunting lodge into the palace and moved the royal court there in 1682.

q: Which Bronze Age palace on Crete is linked to the legend of the Minotaur and the labyrinth?
fact: It was the center of the Minoan civilization, which flourished on Crete about 3,500 years ago.

q: Which machine with turning sails, once used to pump water off the land, is a symbol of the Dutch countryside?
fact: The 19 that stand together at Kinderdijk, built in the 1700s, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: Which white, star-shaped flower of the high Alps is a symbol of both Switzerland and Austria?
fact: Its name means 'noble white' in German, and it appears on Austria's 2-cent euro coin.

q: Which prickly purple flower is the national emblem of Scotland?
fact: It gives its name to the Order of the Thistle, Scotland's highest order of chivalry.

q: Which ice sport, first played in Scotland, slides heavy granite stones toward a target called the house?
fact: Many of the stones used at the Olympics are cut from granite from Ailsa Craig, a tiny Scottish island.

q: Which long-distance running race, about 42 km long, is named after a town in Greece?
fact: Its exact length, 42.195 km, comes from the course of the 1908 London Olympics.

q: What name is given to the Norse seafarers who sailed from Scandinavia to trade, raid and settle from about AD 800?
fact: They reached North America about 500 years before Columbus, at L'Anse aux Meadows in today's Canada.

q: What is the name of the vast region that makes up most of the Asian part of this country?
fact: It covers more than 13 million square km - bigger than any country on Earth except Russia itself.

q: Which ski race, weaving between gates down a slope, takes its name from a Norwegian word for 'sloping track'?
fact: Skiers who miss a single gate are out, and the giant version has fewer, wider-spaced gates.

q: Which long black rowing boat carries visitors along the canals of Venice?
fact: There were thousands of them in centuries past. Today a few hundred remain, rowed by licensed gondoliers.

q: Which seasonal wind brings heavy summer rains to India and much of South Asia?
fact: Its name comes from the Arabic word 'mawsim', meaning 'season'.

q: What is the name for the vast, treeless grasslands of Central Asia and Mongolia?
fact: The Eurasian grassland belt stretches about 8,000 km, from Hungary to Mongolia and northern China.

q: Which cold desert covers much of the south of this country?
fact: The first fossil eggs that scientists recognized as dinosaur eggs were found there in 1923.

q: Which is the northernmost of this country's four main islands?
fact: Its largest city, Sapporo, hosted the 1972 Winter Olympics and holds a famous snow festival every February.

q: Which fine white ceramic, first perfected in China, is often simply called 'china' in English?
fact: The city of Jingdezhen has made it for more than 1,000 years and is still known as the porcelain capital.

q: Which ancient Greek and Roman city on this country's Aegean coast has the grand Library of Celsus?
fact: It was also home to the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

q: Which Japanese dish of vinegared rice with raw fish or vegetables is now eaten all over the world?
fact: It began as a way of preserving fish by packing it in fermenting rice.

q: Which martial art, whose name means 'gentle way', was founded in Japan in 1882?
fact: Its founder was Jigoro Kano. It became an Olympic sport at the 1964 Tokyo Games.

q: Which short Japanese poem has three lines of five, seven and five syllables?
fact: Its most famous master, Matsuo Basho, lived in the 1600s and wrote of a frog jumping into an old pond.

q: Which long-necked stringed instrument did Ravi Shankar make famous around the world?
fact: Besides the strings that are plucked, it has 'sympathetic' strings that ring on their own when the others are played.

q: Which long, draped garment, made of several meters of unstitched cloth, is worn by many women across South Asia?
fact: There are dozens of regional ways to drape it, and it is worn for everything from daily work to weddings.

q: Which fried triangular pastry, often filled with spiced potato and peas, is a favorite snack across South Asia?
fact: Similar pastries reached India from Central Asia and the Middle East many centuries ago.

q: Which ball game, played on horseback with long mallets, began in ancient Persia?
fact: It spread across Asia, and British officers who learned it in India in the 1800s took it around the world.

q: Which sweet pastry of paper-thin layers, chopped nuts and syrup is a famous Turkish dessert?
fact: The pistachio version from the city of Gaziantep has protected status in the European Union.

q: Which red flower, called bunga raya, is the national flower of Malaysia?
fact: Its five petals stand for the five principles of the Rukun Negara, the country's national philosophy.

q: Which red-haired great ape lives in the wild only on Borneo and Sumatra?
fact: Its name comes from Malay words meaning 'person of the forest'.

q: Which giant grass is the fastest-growing plant on Earth?
fact: Some kinds can grow almost 1 m in a single day.

q: Which creamy dip of mashed chickpeas, sesame paste, lemon and garlic is eaten across the Middle East?
fact: Its name is simply the Arabic word for 'chickpea'.

q: What name is given to the traditionally nomadic Arab herders of the deserts of the Middle East?
fact: Their name comes from an Arabic word for desert dwellers. Many raised camels and goats and lived in tents woven from goat hair.

q: Which language is the basis of Filipino, the national language of the Philippines?
fact: It has borrowed many words from Spanish and English - 'kotse' for car comes from the Spanish 'coche'.

q: Which huge Buddhist temple from the 800s, on the island of Java, is the largest Buddhist temple in the world?
fact: It is decorated with 504 Buddha statues and more than 2,600 carved stone panels.

q: Which Turkish site of bright white mineral terraces has a name meaning 'cotton castle'?
fact: Visitors wade through its warm pools, and the ruins of the ancient spa city of Hierapolis lie just above.

q: What is the largest hot desert on Earth?
fact: Its name comes from the Arabic word for 'desert'. Most of it is bare rock and gravel rather than sand dunes.

q: Which is the fourth-longest river in Africa, flowing east through Mozambique into the Indian Ocean?
fact: Along the way it plunges over Victoria Falls and fills the huge dam lakes of Kariba and Cahora Bassa.

q: Which very long African lake, the second deepest in the world, is shared by four countries?
fact: It is about 670 km long - the longest freshwater lake in the world - and is shared by Tanzania, DR Congo, Burundi and Zambia.

q: Which big African animal's name comes from Greek words meaning 'river horse'?
fact: It spends hot days in the water and comes out at night to graze, often walking several kilometers.

q: What is the largest living bird?
fact: It cannot fly, but it can run at about 70 km/h, and its egg weighs about 1.4 kg.

q: Which African tree with a massive trunk can store thousands of liters of water and live for over 1,000 years?
fact: It is sometimes called the 'upside-down tree', because its bare branches look like roots.

q: What is the largest living primate, found in the forests of central Africa?
fact: It is mostly a gentle plant-eater. A big adult male, called a silverback, can weigh close to 200 kg.

q: What title was given to the kings of ancient Egypt?
fact: The word comes from the Egyptian 'per-aa', meaning 'great house' - first the palace, later the king himself.

q: Which tall reed, growing along the Nile, did ancient Egyptians use to make a kind of paper?
fact: The English word 'paper' comes from its name.

q: Which spice island off this country's coast has an old quarter, Stone Town, that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
fact: In the 1800s its farms, together with those of nearby Pemba Island, grew most of the world's cloves.

q: What is the stiff maize-flour porridge called that is eaten with almost every meal in Kenya and Tanzania?
fact: It is rolled into a ball with the fingers and used to scoop up stews and greens. In Uganda a similar dish is called posho.

q: Which dried, cured meat, cut into strips, is a favorite snack across southern Africa?
fact: Early settlers dried meat with vinegar, salt and spices such as coriander so it would keep on long journeys.

q: Which language, which grew out of Dutch, is spoken as a first language by millions in South Africa and Namibia?
fact: It is one of South Africa's official languages, and English borrowed words such as 'aardvark' and 'trek' from it.

q: Which people make up the largest ethnic group in South Africa?
fact: About a quarter of South Africans speak isiZulu as their first language - more than any other language.

q: Which Saharan people are known for the indigo-dyed veils worn by their men?
fact: The dye can rub off on the skin, which is why they are sometimes called 'the blue people' of the desert.

q: Which goblet-shaped hand drum, carved from one piece of wood, comes from West Africa?
fact: It began among the Mande peoples of Mali and Guinea. A skilled player can make deep bass notes and sharp slaps on one drum.

q: Which oil comes from the nuts of a tree that grows wild almost only in southwest Morocco?
fact: It is used in cooking and cosmetics, and local goats are famous for climbing the trees to eat the fruit.

q: What is the longest mountain range on land, running down the western side of South America?
fact: It stretches about 7,000 km through seven countries, from Venezuela to the southern tip of Argentina and Chile.

q: Which great river flows south through the middle of this country, past Memphis and New Orleans?
fact: Its name comes from an Ojibwe word meaning 'great river'.

q: Which Venezuelan lake, according to satellite data, gets more lightning than any other place on Earth?
fact: The storms, known as Catatumbo lightning, form near where the Catatumbo River enters the lake, on well over 100 nights a year.

q: What is a narrow strip of land joining two larger land areas called, like the one at Panama?
fact: Another famous one, the Isthmus of Corinth, joins mainland Greece to the Peloponnese.

q: Which woolly relative of the camel has carried loads in the Andes for thousands of years?
fact: Its smaller cousin, the alpaca, is raised mainly for its soft wool.

q: On the flag of Mexico, the eagle eating a snake is perched on what kind of plant?
fact: It is a prickly pear, or nopal, recalling the Aztec legend of where to build their capital, Tenochtitlan.

q: Which spotted big cat is the largest cat in the Americas?
fact: It has the strongest bite for its size of any big cat - strong enough to crack turtle shells.

q: Which narrow covered boat, moved with a double-bladed paddle, was invented by Arctic peoples?
fact: The first ones were made of driftwood or whalebone frames covered with sealskin.

q: Which salamander, which keeps its feathery gills its whole life, lives in the wild only in canals near Mexico City?
fact: It can regrow lost legs and even parts of its heart, so scientists study it closely.

q: Which lively partner dance grew out of Cuban son music among Latin musicians in New York in the 1960s and 70s?
fact: Its name means 'sauce' in Spanish - a spicy mix of Caribbean styles.

q: Which spirit is distilled from the blue agave plant in Mexico?
fact: It is named after a town in Jalisco, and only drinks from certain regions of Mexico may use the name.

q: Which dish of raw fish 'cooked' in lime juice is Peru's national dish?
fact: Peru celebrates it with a national day every June 28.

q: Which empire, ruled from Cusco, was the largest in the Americas before the Spanish arrived?
fact: Its road network ran for about 30,000 km through the Andes, with rope bridges across deep gorges.

q: Which ancient city near Mexico City is home to the Pyramids of the Sun and the Moon?
fact: Around AD 500 it was one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps 100,000 people.

q: Which district of Los Angeles gave its name to the American film industry?
fact: Its famous hillside sign went up in 1923 to advertise a housing development called 'Hollywoodland'.

q: Which wild, windswept region covers the south of this country and of neighboring Chile?
fact: It has huge glaciers, jagged peaks like Fitz Roy, and more sheep and penguins than people in many places.

q: What are the skilled horseback cattle herders of the South American pampas called?
fact: They are heroes of Argentina's national poem, Martin Fierro, and their traditions live on in rodeos and festivals.

q: Which stick-and-ball game was first played by Indigenous peoples of North America and is Canada's national summer sport?
fact: The Haudenosaunee Nationals compete in world championships as a team of their own.

q: What is the three-pointed spear head in the center of this flag called?
fact: It is the trident of Neptune. Its broken shaft stands for the break from colonial rule at independence in 1966.

q: Which wooden instrument, like a giant xylophone, is the national instrument of Guatemala?
fact: Several players often share one big instrument, each covering a different range of notes.

q: What is a ring-shaped coral reef or chain of islands around a lagoon called?
fact: Charles Darwin first explained how they form: a coral reef keeps growing upward while an old volcano slowly sinks beneath it.

q: Which animal holds up Australia's coat of arms, standing opposite the emu?
fact: One popular story says both were chosen because neither can easily walk backward - a country moving forward.

q: Which tree-dwelling marsupial eats almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves?
fact: It sleeps up to 20 hours a day, because its leafy diet gives it very little energy.

q: Which flightless, night-time bird is a national symbol of New Zealand?
fact: Its egg is huge for its size - up to a fifth of the mother's body weight.

q: Which small, smiling marsupial lives mainly on Rottnest Island off Western Australia?
fact: Dutch sailors mistook them for giant rats, which is how the island got its name - 'rat's nest'.

q: What do Australians call the vast, remote, dry interior of their country?
fact: It covers most of the continent but holds few people. Children on remote farms once had lessons by radio.

q: Which meringue dessert, named after a Russian ballerina, do Australia and New Zealand both claim as their own?
fact: Anna Pavlova toured both countries in 1926, and both say they invented the dessert in her honor.

q: Which Australian cake is a sponge square dipped in chocolate and rolled in coconut?
fact: It is thought to be named after Lord Lamington, governor of Queensland around 1900.

q: Which sheep breed, prized for its very fine wool, has long been the backbone of Australia's wool industry?
fact: The breed was developed in Spain, which for centuries banned the export of its sheep.

q: Which Polynesian people were the first to settle New Zealand?
fact: They arrived by canoe more than 700 years ago. Their language, te reo, is an official language of the country.

q: Which curved throwing stick, used by Aboriginal Australians, can be made to fly back to the thrower?
fact: Only some kinds come back. Heavier hunting ones were made to fly straight and far.

q: Outside Hawaii, what is the Polynesian cloth made by beating the bark of the paper mulberry tree usually called?
fact: In Tonga it is called ngatu and in Samoa siapo. It is painted with bold patterns and given at weddings and other ceremonies.

q: Which chocolate fudge ball, rolled in sprinkles, is served at almost every Brazilian birthday party?
fact: It is said to be named after an air force brigadier, Eduardo Gomes, whose supporters sold the sweets in the 1940s.

q: Which spice, the seed of a tree that once grew only on Indonesia's tiny Banda Islands, made them hugely valuable to traders?
fact: In 1667 the Dutch kept the nutmeg island of Run and in return gave up their claim to Manhattan, in today's New York.

q: Which fruit does Ecuador export more of than any other country in the world?
fact: Almost all bananas sold abroad are a single variety, the Cavendish, picked green and shipped cold so they ripen on arrival.
